name: Modifiability
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Why Upgrading a Blockchain Is Harder Than Upgrading an App: Modifiability
lesson.summary: Modifiability measures how easily a system can be changed after deployment without breaking it, and blockchain architectures make that quality attribute unusually expensive and politically difficult because there is no central deploy button, only thousands of independent operators who each have to agree to run the new code.
lesson.body:
In ordinary software, modifiability means how much it costs, in engineering time and risk, to make a change once a system is already running in production. A well designed codebase lets a team fix a bug or add a feature by touching a small, well isolated part of the system. A poorly designed one forces every change to ripple unpredictably through unrelated parts of the code. This is a standard quality attribute in general software architecture, and it applies to a blockchain's own client software just as it applies to any other program.

What makes blockchain modifiability genuinely different, and considerably harder, is that a change is not deployed by one team pushing code to one server. It has to be adopted by every full node operator independently choosing to run the new version, which turns a technical decision into something closer to a political one. Bitcoin's Segregated Witness upgrade in 2017 is a real example of a soft fork, a change designed to remain compatible with nodes that had not yet upgraded, precisely because backward compatibility lowers the coordination cost of getting a change adopted. Ethereum's response to the DAO hack in 2016, by contrast, was a hard fork, a change incompatible with the old rules, and it required enough of the community and the mining power to agree to abandon the pre hack chain history that a minority who disagreed split off entirely, continuing the original chain as what is now called Ethereum Classic. Both episodes show the same underlying fact: modifiability at the protocol level is bounded not just by code quality but by how much of a decentralized community can be brought to agree.

Smart contracts add another layer to this problem. Code deployed to a chain like Ethereum is immutable by default once it is live, which is often described as a feature, since it is exactly what gives users confidence that the rules cannot be quietly changed underneath them. But it also means a team that discovers a bug after launch has no way to patch it unless they designed for that possibility in advance, typically through an upgradeability pattern such as a proxy contract that lets an administrator point users toward new logic while preserving the original contract address.

That kind of designed in upgradeability is itself an architectural tradeoff, not a free improvement. An upgradeable contract necessarily has an administrator key or a governance process capable of changing the contract's behavior, and that capability is exactly the kind of centralized control point that a security attribute analysis has to treat as an attack surface, since anyone who compromises or coerces the holder of that key can rewrite the rules for every user of the contract. A team gains modifiability and gives up some of the trust guarantee that decentralization was supposed to provide in the first place.

This is a clean example of the tradeoff discipline this chapter keeps returning to. There is no version of a smart contract that is maximally modifiable and maximally trustless at the same time, and pretending otherwise just hides the choice rather than making it. The honest approach is to decide, explicitly and with the relevant stakeholders, how much modifiability a given contract actually needs, weighed openly against the security cost of the mechanism that would provide it.
